items.s: Only the employer may contribute; employees cannot add their own money to the account.
items.w: Only the employer, not the employee, can contribute to a SEP-IRA.

items.s: Employees may elect salary-reduction contributions in addition to the employer’s money.
items.w: A SIMPLE IRA lets employees make their own salary-reduction contributions on top of the employer’s.

items.s: Employer contributions are required.
items.w: SIMPLE IRA employer contributions are required, whereas a SEP-IRA is at the employer’s option.

items.s: Employer contributions are never required; the employer may fund the plan at its option.
items.w: SEP-IRAs are at the option of the employer and are never required.

items.s: Available to companies with no more than 100 eligible employees.
items.w: The SIMPLE IRA is the plan limited to companies with 100 employees or fewer.

items.s: An employer wants a plan in which employee paychecks can never be reduced for retirement savings.
items.w: Because only the employer contributes to a SEP-IRA, employees cannot defer any of their pay.

items.s: A 60-employee firm wants workers able to defer salary while the firm is obliged to contribute.
items.w: Required employer money plus optional employee deferrals describes a SIMPLE IRA for small firms.

items.s: Inexpensive for small businesses to maintain, with the employer alone funding each participant’s IRA.
items.w: A SEP-IRA is cheap to set up and is funded only by the employer.

items.s: The employer bears the investment risk and must add money if returns fall short.
items.w: In a defined benefit plan the employer carries all investment responsibility and funds any shortfall.

items.s: The participant bears the investment risk of the investments chosen.
items.w: In defined contribution plans such as the 401(k), employees bear the investment risk.

items.s: An actuary calculates the annual contributions needed to fund promised future benefits.
items.w: Defined benefit plans require an actuary to determine the funding for promised benefits.

items.s: No minimum benefit is promised; income depends on contributions and investment performance.
items.w: Defined contribution plans promise no minimum benefit, only what the account has grown to.

items.s: Assets sit in one professionally managed trust with no individual employee accounts.
items.w: Defined benefit plans pool company contributions in a trust rather than individual accounts.

items.s: The employee may defer part of salary and direct his own investment choices.
items.w: Elective deferrals and participant-directed investing are features of 401(k)-type defined contribution plans.

items.s: The plan can become underfunded, with too few assets to pay promised retirement obligations.
items.w: An underfunded pension is a defined benefit risk because the benefit is promised in advance.

items.s: The employer may match deferrals or add optional profit-sharing amounts to workers’ accounts.
items.w: Matching and profit-sharing contributions go into individual accounts in defined contribution plans.

items.s: The first required minimum distribution is due by April 1 after the owner turns 73.
items.w: Traditional IRA owners must start RMDs by April 1 of the year after turning 73.

items.s: No required minimum distributions are due during the owner’s lifetime.
items.w: Roth IRAs never require RMDs while the owner is alive; death triggers the requirement.

items.s: Contributions are allowed only if the taxpayer’s income is below a stated limit.
items.w: Roth IRA contributions are limited to taxpayers with income below a certain level.

items.s: Contributions may be tax-deductible, depending on workplace plan coverage and income.
items.w: A traditional IRA can be pre-tax or after-tax depending on plan eligibility and income.

items.s: Contributions are always made with after-tax dollars.
items.w: Roth IRA contributions are never deductible and are always after-tax.

items.s: When contributions were pre-tax, every dollar distributed is taxed as ordinary income.
items.w: Deductible traditional IRAs work like qualified plans, so all distributions are ordinary income.

items.s: Earnings come out completely tax-free only after the five-year period and age 59½.
items.w: Qualified Roth distributions must meet both the five-year test and the age 59½ test.

items.s: An owner covered by a workplace plan whose income is over the threshold can still contribute, but only with non-deductible dollars.
items.w: A traditional IRA can take after-tax contributions in scenario 3, whereas a high-income taxpayer cannot contribute to a Roth at all.

items.s: The maximum contribution is set by each state and varies from state to state.
items.w: 529 plans are state-sponsored, so maximum contributions differ across states.

items.s: Contributions are limited to $2,000 per beneficiary per year.
items.w: The Coverdell has a low $2,000 annual limit per beneficiary, unlike 529 plans.

items.s: It is a municipal fund security offered through a state program.
items.w: 529 plans are municipal fund securities; the Coverdell is not one.

items.s: Funds must be spent or moved to a family member by the time the beneficiary turns 30.
items.w: Coverdell assets unused by age 30 face income tax plus a 10% penalty.

items.s: There is no age limit on the beneficiary.
items.w: Unlike a Coverdell, a 529 plan has no age limit on its beneficiary.

items.s: Available only to families whose income is below a certain level.
items.w: Coverdell availability is restricted by an income limit; 529 plans carry no such restriction.

items.s: Any adult can open one for an existing child, with no earned income requirement.
items.w: A 529 plan can be opened by any adult without earned income for an existing child.

items.s: The beneficiary must be under age 18 when the account is opened.
items.w: A Coverdell is opened for a student under 18, whereas a 529 plan has no age limit on its beneficiary.

title: 10% early penalty vs 25% RMD excise tax

items.s: Applies to a withdrawal taken before age 59½ unless an exception applies.
items.w: The 10% penalty targets early distributions made before age 59½ without an exception.

items.s: Applies when an owner fails to take a required minimum distribution.
items.w: Missing an RMD triggers the excise tax on the under-distributed amount.

items.s: Calculated on the amount withdrawn; a $20,000 withdrawal costs $2,000.
items.w: The early withdrawal penalty is 10% of the withdrawal, so $20,000 yields $2,000.

items.s: Calculated on the under-distributed amount; a $4,000 shortfall left uncorrected costs $1,000.
items.w: The excise tax is 25% of the shortfall, so $4,000 uncorrected costs $1,000.

items.s: Waived for disability, first-time home purchase up to $10,000, or birth or adoption up to $5,000.
items.w: These are listed exceptions to the 10% early withdrawal penalty.

items.s: Reduced to 10% if the shortfall is corrected within the next two years.
items.w: The excise tax falls from 25% to 10% when the under-distribution is corrected within two years.

items.s: A 52-year-old who withdraws IRA money to buy a boat owes this on top of income tax.
items.w: A pre-59½ withdrawal with no exception triggers the 10% penalty plus ordinary income tax.

items.s: A 75-year-old who withdraws less than the calculated amount owes this tax on the difference.
items.w: An owner past the RMD age who under-distributes owes the excise tax on the shortfall.

title: Straight life vs life with period certain

items.s: Pays the highest monthly amount of the payout options because it carries the most risk.
items.w: Straight life has the shortest expected duration and therefore the highest monthly income.

items.s: A beneficiary can still receive payments if the annuitant dies early in the contract.
items.w: The period certain guarantees payments to the annuitant or the beneficiary for a minimum time.

items.s: Nothing is ever paid to a beneficiary after the annuitant’s death.
items.w: Under straight life no payments are made to the beneficiary upon death.

items.s: The beneficiary is protected only during the guaranteed period, commonly 10 or 15 years.
items.w: Beneficiary protection under this option lasts only for the period certain, often 10 or 15 years.

items.s: If the annuitant dies after a single payment, the insurer owes nothing further.
items.w: Even after only one payment, the insurer has no further obligation under straight life.

items.s: Guarantees a minimum number of years of payments, whoever receives them.
items.w: The period certain sets a minimum payment period to the annuitant or the beneficiary.

items.s: With a 10-year guarantee, an annuitant who dies after year 6 leaves the beneficiary four more years of payments.
items.w: The beneficiary collects the remaining four years of the 10-year period certain.

items.s: Must meet ERISA requirements, including a fiduciary and a vesting schedule.
items.w: Qualified plans must satisfy ERISA, which requires a fiduciary, non-discrimination and vesting.

items.s: The employer chooses which employees participate, often favoring key executives.
items.w: Non-qualified plans are outside ERISA, so employers pick participants and reward executives.

items.s: Contributions are pre-tax and tax-deductible.
items.w: Qualified plans allow pre-tax contributions, giving the immediate tax deduction.

items.s: Contributions are after-tax and non-deductible to the company.
items.w: Non-qualified plans use after-tax contributions and give no immediate deduction.

items.s: Every dollar distributed is taxed as ordinary income.
items.w: With pre-tax contributions, the whole distribution is ordinary income in a qualified plan.

items.s: Only the growth above the contributions is taxed as ordinary income at distribution.
items.w: Because contributions were after-tax, only the growth is taxed in a non-qualified plan.

items.s: If the employer becomes insolvent, plan assets can be claimed by creditors.
items.w: Non-qualified plan assets are unprotected in bankruptcy, creating credit risk for the employee.

items.s: Must be offered on a non-discriminatory basis to full-time employees age 21 with one year of service.
items.w: ERISA’s non-discrimination rule applies to qualified plans, not to non-qualified plans.
